  "title": "Does Error-Type Conditioning Improve GRPO-Based Agent Recovery?",
  "core_problem": "Fission-GRPO (ACL 2026) established that error-triggered GRPO resampling—fissioning each failed tool-call trajectory into G' parallel recovery attempts—improves agent recovery on BFCL v4 Multi-Turn by +5.7% absolute recovery rate. However, Fission-GRPO treats all errors uniformly: every fission event receives the same resampling budget G' regardless of error type, and advantages are normalized within each fission group without regard to error category. Three concurrent lines of work suggest this uniformity is suboptimal. Stratified GRPO (arXiv:2510.06214) demonstrates that structurally heterogeneous GRPO groups suffer cross-stratum advantage bias, corrected by stratified advantage normalization (SAN). CoBA-RL (arXiv:2602.03048), Knapsack RL (arXiv:2509.25849), and BranPO (arXiv:2602.03719) show that difficulty-proportional rollout or branching budget allocation consistently outperforms uniform allocation in GRPO training for reasoning and search agents. ToolScan (arXiv:2509.25370) characterizes seven distinct error patterns in tool-use LLMs, with empirical evidence that error type distributions vary significantly across models—IFN (incorrect function name) and IAC (insufficient API calls) dominate for many models, while IFE (format errors) varies widely. These error types have demonstrably different recovery difficulty profiles, yet no method conditions recovery training budget or advantage computation on error category. Does error-type-conditioned budget allocation and advantage stratification improve over Fission-GRPO's uniform error-triggered resampling, and if so, for which error types does conditioning matter most?",
  "opportunity": "A specific methodological gap exists at the intersection of three established ideas, each validated independently but never combined. (1) Error-triggered resampling for recovery (Fission-GRPO, ACL 2026): fissions failed trajectories into G' recovery attempts with uniform budget—effective but type-agnostic. (2) Stratified advantage normalization (Stratified GRPO, arXiv:2510.06214): eliminates cross-stratum bias by normalizing advantages within structural strata—but uses trajectory structure (search call count), not error categories. (3) Difficulty-proportional budget allocation (CoBA-RL, arXiv:2602.03048; BranPO, arXiv:2602.03719): allocates more rollouts or branching depth to harder tasks—but operates at task or episode level, not error-type level. The specific combination—error-type-conditioned budget for recovery resampling (K_τ ∝ 1-RR_pilot(τ), more fission branches for harder-to-recover error types) plus error-type-stratified advantage normalization (preventing easy-to-recover errors from dominating gradients over hard-to-recover errors)—is absent from all prior work. This matters because: (a) uniform budget wastes exploration on easy recoveries while under-exploring hard ones, and (b) cross-type advantage bias systematically penalizes recovery attempts for hard error types when normalized against easy ones. Additionally, error-type conditioning enables per-type empirical analysis of RL-based recovery training—revealing which error categories benefit from RL-based branching vs. SFT-based relabeling and how type-conditioned budget interacts with recovery difficulty—a diagnostic contribution absent from prior RL-based recovery work. (PALADIN's evaluation framework supports per-class metric reporting across ToolScan categories in principle (Appendix J.3), but reports only aggregate metrics and uses SFT rather than RL; no work has analyzed per-type recovery dynamics under RL training with type-conditioned budgets.) A further practical advantage: by using raw environment error traces (which BFCL v4 provides natively with up to 20 retries) instead of Fission-GRPO's trained Error Simulator (requiring 2K Claude-annotated examples + Qwen3-32B SFT), our approach is annotation-free and simpler to deploy—though this trades some recovery signal quality for zero annotation cost, as Fission-GRPO's ablation shows the Error Simulator provides +2.75% over static error messages on Qwen3-8B.",
  "landscape": "Fission-GRPO (ACL 2026, arXiv:2601.15625) is the most directly related work: it fissions each failed trajectory into G' parallel recovery attempts augmented with diagnostic feedback from a trained Error Simulator (Qwen3-32B SFT on 2K Claude Sonnet 4-written examples), achieving +4.0% overall accuracy and +5.7% recovery rate on BFCL v4 Multi-Turn with Qwen3-8B. Critically, it uses uniform resampling budget G' for all error types and does not condition on error category—the Error Simulator generates context-aware feedback but does not classify errors. No code has been publicly released (as of May 2026), which adds reimplementation risk for the uniform-fission baseline. Stratified GRPO (arXiv:2510.06214, ICLR 2026 submission) proposes Stratified Advantage Normalization (SAN), which partitions GRPO trajectories into strata by structural properties (number of search calls) and normalizes advantages within each stratum, eliminating cross-stratum bias. Applied to search agents on QA benchmarks (NQ, HotpotQA, MuSiQue) with Qwen-2.5-3B, achieving up to +11.3 points over standard GRPO. The general mechanism of stratified normalization is established, but its application to error-type strata in recovery training is novel. CoBA-RL (arXiv:2602.03048) models task preferences via a Beta distribution with capability-aware parameters, allocating more rollout budget to tasks at the model's learning frontier—outperforms Knapsack RL (arXiv:2509.25849) on math reasoning. Both operate at task difficulty level, not error-type level. BranPO (arXiv:2602.03719) introduces difficulty-aware contrastive branch sampling for multi-turn search agents, adapting branching frequency based on group-level accuracy: easy tasks (100% accuracy) receive 1 branch while hard tasks trigger up to 3 recursive branching levels. This is conceptually parallel to ETC-Fission's K_τ ∝ 1-RR_pilot(τ), but BranPO targets search agents rather than tool-use recovery and conditions on task-level accuracy rather than error-type-level recovery difficulty. Code available at github.com/YubaoZhao/BranPO. AERO (arXiv:2602.14338) uses a probe-based stratification and Bayesian posterior to adaptively allocate rollout budgets in GRPO, reducing training compute by ~48% while matching performance. Applied to math reasoning (Qwen2.5-Math), not tool-use, but demonstrates that adaptive allocation is broadly effective for GRPO. GiGPO (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv:2505.10978) achieves fine-grained step-level credit assignment in GRPO for agents via anchor state grouping—constructing step-level contrastive groups by identifying repeated environment states across trajectories. Gains >12% on ALFWorld and >9% on WebShop over standard GRPO. Relevant as a GRPO extension that addresses credit assignment granularity for agents, though it does not condition on error type. RC-GRPO (arXiv:2602.03025) addresses within-group reward variance collapse in multi-turn tool calling via reward-conditioned trajectory generation, achieving 85.0% on BFCL v4 with Qwen2.5-7B—a strong result but on a different axis (variance vs. type conditioning). PALADIN (ICLR 2026, arXiv:2509.25238) trains recovery via SFT on 50K+ GPT-5-annotated trajectories across ToolScan's 7 error categories, achieving 89.68% recovery rate. Its evaluation framework supports per-class reporting of RR, TSR, CSR, and ES across ToolScan categories (Appendix J.3), though the paper reports only aggregate metrics. PALADIN demonstrates that error-category-aware training data construction helps recovery, but uses SFT (not RL) and does not analyze per-type recovery dynamics or the interaction between type-conditioned budgets and recovery difficulty. 'Failure Makes Agent Stronger' (arXiv:2509.18847) uses DAPO+GSPO on synthetic errors with ~18 person-days human annotation. AgentHER (arXiv:2603.21357) uses hindsight experience replay with failure-severity weighting for SFT-based recovery. GVPO (OpenReview 2026) uses process-verifiable signals as step-level reward shaping but treats errors as generic process rewards without taxonomy. AT²PO (arXiv:2601.04767) and A²TGPO (arXiv:2605.06200) use entropy-based turn-level branching for search agents. InfoTree (arXiv:2605.05262) uses submodular budget allocation—principled but domain-agnostic. ARPO (ICLR 2026, arXiv:2507.19849) and Tree-GRPO (ICLR 2026, arXiv:2509.21240) establish entropy-triggered and uniform branching respectively. ToolScan (arXiv:2509.25370) defines 7 error patterns (IAC, IAV, IAN, IAT, RAC, IFN, IFE) used for evaluation but not for conditioning RL training; empirical data shows IFN is the most common error for many models and error distributions vary significantly across model families. ERR Measure (arXiv:2601.22352) formalizes recovery metrics. HiPER (arXiv:2602.16165) near-saturates ALFWorld (97.4%). CLEANER (arXiv:2601.15141) purifies trajectories via adaptive rollback but does not condition on error type. The specific intersection—error-type-conditioned budget allocation + error-type-stratified advantage normalization within error-triggered GRPO resampling for recovery—remains unoccupied.",
  "approach": "We propose Error-Type-Conditioned Fission (ETC-Fission), an extension of Fission-GRPO that adds error-type conditioning to error-triggered GRPO resampling for recovery training, evaluated on BFCL v4 Multi-Turn. The method has three components:\n\n(1) Error-Type Classification and Type-Conditioned Budget Allocation: When the policy model (Qwen3-8B) encounters execution errors during rollout on BFCL v4 Multi-Turn, we classify each error into one of 5 categories using rule-based parsing of BFCL v4's structured error traces: (a) format error (malformed JSON/function call syntax), (b) incorrect function name (calling non-existent or wrong function), (c) argument type/value error (correct function but wrong parameters), (d) missing argument error, (e) function unavailable (for miss_func scenarios). Unlike Fission-GRPO which uses uniform G' for all fission events, we allocate the fission budget K_τ per error type τ proportional to recovery difficulty: K_τ = round(K_base · (1 - RR_pilot(τ)) / Z), where RR_pilot(τ) is the recovery rate for error type τ from a pilot run (500 trajectories), and Z is a normalization constant ensuring total budget matches the uniform baseline. This applies CoBA-RL/BranPO's principle of difficulty-proportional allocation at the error-type granularity rather than task or episode granularity. Harder-to-recover error types receive more recovery branches, concentrating exploration budget where uniform allocation under-explores.\n\nMinimum sample threshold: We enforce n_min ≥ 30 instances per error-type stratum for valid statistical analysis. During the pilot run, if an error type has fewer than 30 instances, it is merged into an 'other' category. We report which types were merged and at what counts, enabling readers to assess statistical validity. Based on ToolScan's empirical data showing that IFN (incorrect function name) and IAC (insufficient API calls) are the most frequent error types across models, we expect 3-4 types to meet the threshold with 500 pilot trajectories, with IFE and IAT potentially requiring merging.\n\n(2) Error-Type-Stratified Advantage Normalization: Following Stratified GRPO's insight that cross-stratum advantage bias distorts gradient contributions, we stratify GRPO advantages by error type. Within each fission group, advantages are z-score normalized within the error-type stratum rather than globally across all fission groups: A_stratified(τ_i) = (R(τ_i) - μ_k) / (σ_k + ε), where k is the error type of the fission event producing τ_i. This prevents easy-to-recover error types from dominating the advantage signal over hard-to-recover types. We use Stratified GRPO's blended formulation (α-weighted combination of stratified and global advantages) for finite-sample stability when some error types have few instances—particularly important for rare types near the n_min threshold. This is a domain-specific instantiation of SAN: Stratified GRPO uses trajectory structure (search count) as the stratification variable; we use error category.\n\n(3) Annotation-Free Error Feedback via Native Error Traces: Unlike Fission-GRPO which trains an Error Simulator (Qwen3-32B SFT on 2K Claude Sonnet 4-annotated examples) to generate diagnostic feedback, we use BFCL v4's native error traces directly as the recovery context. BFCL v4 provides structured error messages (function not found, type mismatch, missing required parameter, etc.) with up to 20 retries per error. We acknowledge this is a simplicity-performance tradeoff: Fission-GRPO's ablation shows the Error Simulator provides +2.75% over static error messages on Qwen3-8B. Our annotation-free approach trades this signal quality for zero annotation cost and simpler deployment—a tradeoff we consider acceptable for a short paper focused on the orthogonal question of type conditioning. The fission context is constructed as [query; failed_trajectory; environment_error_trace] without synthetic augmentation. If the annotation-free approach substantially underperforms, we note that type conditioning can be combined with the Error Simulator in future work—the two contributions are independent.\n\nSystematic Comparison: We compare six conditions: (a) ETC-Fission (ours: type-conditioned budget + type-stratified advantages + native error traces), (b) Uniform-Fission (uniform budget G' + global advantages + native error traces—our reimplementation of Fission-GRPO's core mechanism without the Error Simulator), (c) Type-Budget-Only (type-conditioned budget + global advantages, isolating the budget allocation contribution), (d) Type-Stratified-Only (uniform budget + type-stratified advantages, isolating the SAN contribution), (e) standard GRPO (no fission), (f) AgentHER (SFT on hindsight-relabeled failed trajectories). All methods use Qwen3-8B with LoRA, 1 iterative round. Since Fission-GRPO's code is not publicly available, we implement the uniform-fission baseline from the paper description (LIFO buffer, correctness threshold, fission group generation with native error traces); we clearly note this is our reimplementation without the Error Simulator.\n\nExpected Improvement and Positioning: We set realistic expectations: based on difficulty-proportional allocation improvements in math reasoning (CoBA-RL, Knapsack RL: typically 1-3% absolute) and BranPO's gains on search (2-3% F1), we expect ETC-Fission to yield a modest 1-2% absolute improvement over uniform fission on aggregate metrics. This is acceptable because the primary contribution is not the aggregate improvement but the per-type diagnostic analysis: revealing which error categories benefit most from type-conditioned RL branching, which are better served by uniform allocation, and which may be better addressed by SFT relabeling. This per-type analysis of RL-based recovery training—decomposing the interaction between error category, budget allocation, and advantage normalization—is absent from all prior RL-based recovery work (Fission-GRPO, ARPO, Tree-GRPO report only aggregate metrics; PALADIN's evaluation framework supports per-class reporting in principle but presents only aggregate results and uses SFT not RL).\n\nEvaluation: Overall accuracy, Recovery Rate (RR), Post-Error Task Success Rate (PE-TSR), and Recovery Efficiency (steps-to-recover) following ERR measure framework. The central empirical contribution is error-type-stratified analysis: per-type RR/PE-TSR/efficiency breakdown with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, revealing which error types drive the gain from type conditioning. We report per-type sample counts and flag any types merged due to insufficient instances.\n\nPositioning: We build explicitly on Fission-GRPO's paradigm of error-triggered GRPO resampling, extending it with type-conditioned budget allocation (from CoBA-RL/BranPO's difficulty-proportional principle) and type-stratified advantage normalization (from Stratified GRPO's SAN). The contribution is the combination, the per-type RL-based diagnostic analysis, and the simplicity-performance tradeoff of annotation-free error feedback—not the individual components.",

## Reviewer feedback (round 5)
Issues: ["IMPACT CEILING CONCERN: The paper's primary contribution (per-type diagnostic analysis) is contingent on error-type diversity in the data. BFCL v4 does NOT publish per-category error distributions, and no public data exists on Qwen3-8B's error type breakdown on BFCL v4 Multi-Turn. If errors are heavily skewed toward 1-2 types (plausible: ToolScan shows IFN dominates for many models), the per-type analysis degrades to a per-2-types analysis, which is too thin for a primary contribution. The generator should run a quick pilot BEFORE committing to the full experimental plan.", "MISSING WORK — EGCA (arXiv:2603.16158): Execution-Grounded Credit Assignment localizes GRPO updates using execution traces to identify semantic divergence points between candidate and reference solutions. While it focuses on credit assignment rather than error-type budget allocation, it uses execution traces in GRPO training for agents — directly relevant context. Should be cited.", "MISSING WORK — EDGE-GRPO (arXiv:2507.21848): Entropy-Driven GRPO with Guided Error Correction addresses advantage diversity in GRPO via entropy-driven advantages and guided error correction at the signal level. While not error-type-specific, it is relevant as a GRPO variant that addresses the advantage collapse problem that type-stratified normalization also targets. Should be cited.", "NOVELTY CEILING: After accounting for Fission-GRPO (error-triggered GRPO resampling), Stratified GRPO (stratified advantage normalization), and CoBA-RL/BranPO (difficulty-proportional allocation), the unique methodological contribution reduces to: 'apply known proportional allocation and known stratified normalization at error-type granularity instead of task or structure granularity.' This is a valid instantiation but not a deep methodological insight. The K_τ = round(K_base · (1-RR_pilot(τ))/Z) formula is a single line of trivially derived code. For EMNLP Main (even short paper), reviewers may judge this as an ablation study of existing techniques rather than a new method.", "ANNOTATION-FREE FRAMING IS A NET NEGATIVE: The generator positions annotation-free error feedback as 'simpler deployment' but acknowledges it loses 2.75% signal quality. This means the proposed method starts at a disadvantage relative to Fission-GRPO before any type conditioning gains are added. If type conditioning yields only +1-2% and annotation-free loses -2.75%, the net system is WORSE than Fission-GRPO. The generator says the two contributions are independent, but reviewers will ask: what is the combined system's performance relative to full Fission-GRPO?", "EXPECTED NEGATIVE RESULT RISK: If error-type conditioning yields only +1-2% over uniform fission, and this is within the noise margin for some error types (especially with n≈30 per stratum), the paper risks being a null result. While the generator frames this as 'the analysis is the contribution,' null results with modest sample sizes per stratum are very hard to publish at top venues. The paper needs a clear contingency: what is the publishable contribution if type conditioning shows no statistically significant improvement?", "SINGLE BENCHMARK LIMITS GENERALIZABILITY: BFCL v4 Multi-Turn is a function-calling benchmark with structured error traces. The generator's approach relies heavily on BFCL v4's native error message structure for rule-based classification. Findings may not transfer to benchmarks with unstructured errors (WebArena, SWE-bench) or different error distributions. For EMNLP, even a short paper benefits from showing robustness on at least 2 benchmarks."]
Feedback: The idea is well-refined and honestly positioned after 5 rounds, but faces inherent limitations in novelty and impact that put it below the EMNLP Main threshold. The average score (3.0) reflects a solid but unexciting contribution. To push toward 'pass':

1. **ADDRESS THE ANNOTATION-FREE CONFOUND (HIGHEST PRIORITY)**: The annotation-free choice creates a confound that undermines the core research question. If ETC-Fission (type-conditioned + annotation-free) vs. Uniform-Fission (uniform + annotation-free) shows +1-2%, you've answered the type-conditioning question. But reviewers will want to know: does ETC-Fission beat full Fission-GRPO (uniform + Error Simulator)? If not, the practical value is questionable. Consider: (a) frame the paper ONLY as 'type conditioning vs. uniform, holding error feedback constant' and make annotation-free vs. Simulator a separate explicit non-contribution, or (b) include one condition with a simple Error Simulator (even GPT-4o-mini for classification rather than Qwen3-32B SFT) to show type conditioning helps even with better error feedback.

2. **VALIDATE ERROR DIVERSITY BEFORE COMMITTING**: Run 100-200 trajectories with Qwen3-8B on BFCL v4 Multi-Turn (1-2 hours) to check the actual error type distribution. If <3 types have n≥30, pivot: either switch to τ-bench (which has diverse tool-use scenarios) or augment with deliberate error injection. Do NOT commit 14 days to a paper whose primary contribution requires data diversity you haven't verified.

3. **DEEPEN THE K_τ MECHANISM**: The proportional allocation K_τ = round(K_base · (1-RR_pilot(τ))/Z) is too simple to constitute a methodological contribution. Consider: (a) a Bayesian approach like CoBA-RL's Beta distribution, modeling per-type recovery probability with uncertainty and allocating budget based on expected information gain rather than raw difficulty, or (b) adaptive K_τ that updates during training (not just from a one-shot pilot), capturing how type-specific recovery difficulty changes as the model improves. Either would add genuine methodological depth beyond applying existing formulas at a new granularity.

4. **ADD τ-BENCH AS A SECOND BENCHMARK**: τ-bench (mentioned in user requirements) has diverse multi-turn tool-use scenarios with natural error diversity. Even a partial evaluation (e.g., τ-bench retail subset only, ~2-3 extra H100 hours for evaluation) would significantly strengthen generalizability claims. This fits within the compute budget.

5. **CITE EGCA AND EDGE-GRPO**: Add Execution-Grounded Credit Assignment (arXiv:2603.16158, uses execution traces in GRPO) and EDGE-GRPO (arXiv:2507.21848, addresses advantage diversity in GRPO) to the landscape.

6. **PREPARE A NULL-RESULT CONTINGENCY**: If type conditioning shows no statistically significant improvement, the paper could still be valuable as a negative result that reveals error-type conditioning is unnecessary because (a) error types have similar recovery difficulty in practice, or (b) GRPO already implicitly handles type heterogeneity. Frame this possibility explicitly in the introduction — 'whether the answer is positive or negative, it informs future RL-based recovery work.' This is more publishable than an ambiguous +1% with wide CIs.

## Instructions
- Think in two phases: FIRST reconsider the problem framing (core_problem / opportunity / landscape) if the reviewer flagged issues there, THEN revise the method (approach / resource_estimate / key_references). Do not jump straight to fixing the method if the underlying problem framing needs correction.

## Authors

- Shikhar Gupta

# EDGE-GRPO: Key Details

## Title & Authors
**Full Title:** "EDGE-GRPO: Entropy-Driven GRPO with Guided Error Correction for Advantage Diversity"

**Authors:** Xingjian Zhang, Siwei Wen, Wenjun Wu, Lei Huang

## Abstract Summary
The paper addresses a critical limitation in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithms used for LLM reasoning tasks. The researchers note that GRPO's reliance on sparse reward rules frequently produces "identical rewards within groups, leading to the advantage collapse problem."

## Core Problem & Solution
EDGE-GRPO tackles advantage collapse through two complementary strategies:

1. **Entropy-Driven Advantage:** Rather than enforcing model reflection for diversity, the method operates at a fine-grained sample level, analyzing "policy entropy of responses" to naturally encourage varied outputs within training groups.

2. **Guided Error Correction:** This mechanism augments training signals by providing "internal feedback to augment the training signal (advantage)," helping the model learn from mistakes more effectively.

## Approach Rationale
The authors critique existing solutions, finding limitations in reflection-based diversity approaches. Their entropy-focused methodology represents a shift toward intrinsic model behavior rather than external prompting techniques for achieving diverse, advantageous responses across reasoning benchmarks.

## Key Findings:

### AERO (Adaptive Efficient Rollout Optimization)
AERO addresses key inefficiencies in GRPO through adaptive rollout reallocation, theoretically-grounded down-sampling, and Bayesian estimation to avoid gradient dead zones. Under the same total rollout budget, AERO reduces total training compute by about 48% while shortening wall-clock time per step by about 45% on average. AERO was tested across three model configurations (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct).

### VIP (Adaptive Rollout Allocation Framework)
Existing group-based policy optimization methods, such as GRPO, allocate a fixed number of rollouts for all training prompts. This uniform allocation implicitly treats all prompts as equally informative, and could lead to inefficient computational budget usage and impede training progress. VIP enables recursive Bayesian updates that leverage both past rollout outcomes and the similarity structure of the prompts.

### CoBA-RL (Capability-Oriented Budget Allocation)
Complex samples often harbor higher training value and demand extensive exploration, whereas simple instances require minimal resources. Dynamically allocating rollout budgets during reinforcement learning—specifically to optimize the trade-off between exploration and exploitation—remains a significant challenge.

### OptPO (Test-time Policy Optimization)
OptPO formulates early-stopping consensus estimation as a Bayesian sequential probability ratio test, adaptively allocating rollouts based on posterior evidence rather than fixed budgets.

All of these approaches represent recent advances (2025-2026) in addressing computational efficiency in GRPO-based LLM training through principled adaptive allocation mechanisms.

# Adaptive Rollout Allocation for Online Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

## Full Title
"Adaptive Rollout Allocation for Online Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards"

## Authors
Hieu Trung Nguyen, Bao Nguyen, Wenao Ma, Yuzhi Zhao, Ruifeng She, and Viet Anh Nguyen

## Abstract Summary
The paper addresses sampling efficiency in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. The authors critique existing methods that use uniform rollout allocation across all training prompts, arguing this treats all prompts as equally informative and wastes computational resources.

## VIP Method Details

**Core Approach:**
The VIP (Variance-Informed Predictive) allocation strategy dynamically distributes rollout budgets to optimize policy gradient variance. The method employs "a lightweight Gaussian process model to predict per-prompt success probabilities based on recent rollouts."

**Budget Allocation Mechanism:**
Probability predictions from the GP model convert into variance estimates, which feed into a convex optimization problem that determines optimal rollout allocations under a strict compute budget constraint.

**Bayesian Update:**
The paper describes using a Gaussian process—a Bayesian method—to iteratively predict success probabilities from recent rollout data, effectively implementing sequential Bayesian inference.

## Key Results
The paper demonstrates that VIP "consistently improves sampling efficiency and achieves higher performance than uniform or heuristic allocation strategies in multiple benchmarks."

## Publication Status
Accepted at ICLR 2026 (submitted February 2, 2026)

**Authors:** Victor Barres, Honghua Dong, Soham Ray, Xujie Si, Karthik Narasimhan

## Domain Coverage

The benchmark focuses on a **Telecom domain** modeled as a Dec-POMDP (Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process). This dual-control setting represents scenarios like technical support where both the AI agent and user actively modify a shared, dynamic environment.

## Core Contributions

The paper introduces four major components:

1. **Environment design** featuring collaborative interaction between agent and user
2. **Compositional task generator** that programmatically creates diverse, verifiable tasks
3. **User simulator** tightly coupled with the environment, constrained by observable states and available tools
4. **Fine-grained performance analysis** through ablations

## Error Analysis Capabilities

The framework enables researchers to "separate errors arising from reasoning vs communication/coordination." This distinction allows evaluation of whether performance gaps stem from logical reasoning failures or difficulties in guiding user actions.

## Key Finding

"Experiments show significant performance drops when agents shift from no-user to dual-control," highlighting that guiding users represents a substantial challenge distinct from autonomous task completion.

# Paper Summary: Multi-Turn RL for Tool-Calling Agents

## Full Title
"Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning for Tool-Calling Agents with Iterative Reward Calibration"

## Authors
Wachiravit Modecrua, Krittanon Kaewtawee, Krittin Pachtrachai, Touchapon Kraisingkorn

## Core Contribution
This work addresses a fundamental challenge in training conversational agents: designing reward signals that work well across multiple dialogue turns. The authors discovered that naively constructed dense per-turn rewards can actually harm performance by up to 14 percentage points due to misalignment between reward quality metrics and advantage estimates.

## Key Innovation: Iterative Reward Calibration
The paper introduces a methodology for crafting per-turn rewards through "empirical discriminative analysis of rollout data." This approach uses actual training data to ensure rewards properly distinguish between better and worse agent behaviors at each conversation turn.

## Technical Methods
The research combines two optimization algorithms:
- **MT-GRPO** (Multi-Turn Group Relative Policy Optimization) 
- **GTPO** (Generalized Token-level Policy Optimization), featuring a "hybrid advantage formulation" that resolves advantage misalignment problems

## Benchmark Results
Testing on **Tau-Bench** (airline customer service domain):
- Qwen 3.5-4B: 63.8% → 66.7% (+2.9pp)
- Qwen 3-30B-A3B: 58.0% → 69.5% (+11.5pp)
- The 4B model outperformed GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o despite being 50× smaller
- The 30B MoE model approached Claude Sonnet 4.5 performance

These represent the first published RL training results on Tau-Bench.

## Paper Summary: Execution-Grounded Credit Assignment for GRPO in Code Generation (arXiv 2603.16158)

The paper proposes Execution-Grounded Credit Assignment (EGCA), which localizes GRPO updates using execution traces.

**Problem Addressed:** GRPO-style updates suffer from coarse credit assignment: a single outcome signal is spread uniformly across long programs even when failure stems from a localized semantic error.

**Key Approach:** For programs that satisfy algorithmic constraints but fail tests, EGCA executes the candidate and a canonical reference solution (curated once offline; used for analysis, not supervision) under identical instrumentation, identifies the earliest semantic divergence, and assigns advantage only to the corresponding token span while masking downstream tokens.

**Results:** EGCA achieves 82.1% pass@1 on HumanEval (+3.1 over GRPO) and 68.9% on MBPP (+1.5) with 18% wall-clock overhead.

**Key Innovation:** EGCA routes each sample through deterministic failure-mode gates (syntax/constraint/logic) and, for near-correct candidates, localizes the earliest execution divergence against a reference trace to concentrate the GRPO advantage on the causal token span.

EGCA is a drop-in modification requiring no critic, auxiliary loss, or learned verifier.

## Overview of ToolScan

ToolScan is a new benchmark designed to identify error patterns in LLM output on tool-use tasks, with a dataset comprising queries from diverse environments that test for seven newly characterized error patterns.

## Error Patterns Distribution

The error metrics identified in ToolScan occurring in each API call include IAC (Insufficient API Calls), IAV (Incorrect Argument Value), RAC (Repeated API Calls), IFE (Invalid Format Error), IAT (Incorrect Argument Type), IAN (Incorrect Argument Name), and IFN (Incorrect Function Name).

## Qwen Model Findings

The research revealed specific error patterns in Qwen models:

- **Repeated API Calls (RAC)**: Smaller models like DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B perform Repeated API Calls despite clear instructions to avoid repetition, getting stuck in loops based on their internal belief of solving the query.

- **Insufficient API Calls (IAC)**: There is a correlation between RAC and IAC in these models, suggesting that RAC often leads to IAC.

- **Incorrect Argument Value (IAV)**: Models tend to ignore optional arguments like sorting and limit, going with default values set in functions, which can be seen in models like DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B.

## Connection to BFCL

Research on tool calling shows that base models encode the correct tool before they can emit it, recovering 69–82% on BFCL while base generation reaches only 2–10%.

# Error Type Distribution in ToolScan Benchmark

Based on the paper's empirical results, **Table 4** presents comprehensive error metrics across 12 LLMs. Here are the key findings:

## Dominant Error Patterns

**Insufficient API Calls (IAC)** emerges as the most prevalent error type. The paper explicitly states: "We observe that Insufficient API Calls (IAC) is the most common error pattern. Most models have a significantly low IAC score."

Models show particularly low IAC performance:
- DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B: 0.19
- Mixtral-8x7B: 0.11
- Vicuna-13B: 0.27

## Error Distribution Across Models

The highest-performing models (GPT-4, xLAM variants) demonstrate:
- **IFN/IAN scores**: 0.91-0.94 (strong resistance to hallucination)
- **RAC scores**: 0.95-1.00 (minimal repetition)
- **IFE scores**: 0.94-1.00 (format compliance)

Weaker performers like Mistral-7B and Vicuna-13B show:
- **IFN**: 0.60, 0.50
- **IAN**: 0.47, 0.40
- **IAV**: 0.21, 0.61

## Qwen Model Data

The paper includes **DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen variants** (7B and 14B), which exhibited particularly poor performance across most metrics, with success rates of 0.11 and 0.32 respectively.

I now have comprehensive research findings. Let me synthesize my analysis and compose the major revision.

**Key findings from research:**
1. Fission-GRPO code is NOT actually released (placeholder repo) - reimplementation still needed
2. VIP (ICLR 2026) provides a principled Bayesian framework for adaptive rollout allocation using GP
3. τ-bench has 4 structured error types with auto-classification; τ³-bench adds banking domain
4. Multi-turn RL on τ-bench is proven feasible (arXiv:2604.02869)
5. EGCA is an ICLR 2026 Workshop paper on execution-trace-based credit assignment
6. EDGE-GRPO addresses advantage collapse via entropy-driven diversity
7. ToolScan shows IAC is the most prevalent error type; distributions vary significantly by model
8. No existing work does Bayesian adaptive allocation at error-type level

**My assessment:** The core direction (error-type conditioning for GRPO recovery) is valid but needs a major revision to cross the novelty threshold. The trivial K_τ formula, the annotation-free confound, and single-benchmark limitation are fixable through deeper methodology and broader evaluation. A pivot is unnecessary - the research gap is real.

Here is the revised idea:

  "core_problem": "Fission-GRPO (ACL 2026) established that error-triggered GRPO resampling—fissioning each failed trajectory into G' parallel recovery attempts—improves agent recovery on BFCL v4 Multi-Turn by +5.7% absolute recovery rate. However, Fission-GRPO treats all errors uniformly: every fission event receives the same resampling budget G' regardless of error type, and advantages are normalized globally across all fission groups without regard to error category. Three lines of evidence suggest this uniformity is suboptimal. First, Stratified GRPO (arXiv:2510.06214) demonstrates that structurally heterogeneous GRPO groups suffer cross-stratum advantage bias, correctable by stratified advantage normalization. Second, VIP (ICLR 2026, arXiv:2602.01601), CoBA-RL (arXiv:2602.03048), and BranPO (arXiv:2602.03719) show that difficulty-proportional or Bayesian-adaptive rollout allocation consistently outperforms uniform allocation in GRPO training. Third, ToolScan (arXiv:2509.25370) characterizes seven distinct error patterns in tool-use LLMs with empirically heterogeneous distributions across models—IAC (insufficient API calls) dominates overall, while IFN (incorrect function name) and IAV (incorrect argument value) show high model-dependent variation. Critically, a dimension that prior work on adaptive allocation (VIP, CoBA-RL, AERO) has overlooked: per-type recovery difficulty is non-stationary during training. As the policy improves, it may rapidly learn to recover from format errors while struggling persistently with incorrect function names, meaning static allocation—whether uniform or pilot-estimated—fails to track the shifting recovery frontier. The method has three components, evaluated on BFCL v4 Multi-Turn and τ-bench retail.\n\n(1) Bayesian Adaptive Error-Type Budget Allocation via Thompson Sampling: When the policy model (Qwen3-8B) encounters execution errors during rollout, we classify each error into one of T categories using rule-based parsing of the benchmark's structured error traces. For BFCL v4: format error, incorrect function name, argument type/value error, missing argument, function unavailable. For τ-bench: used_wrong_tool, used_wrong_tool_argument, goal_partially_completed, took_unintended_action. For each error type τ ∈ {1,...,T}, we maintain a Beta posterior Beta(α_τ, β_τ) over the recovery probability p_τ, initialized with weak prior α_τ = β_τ = 1. At each training iteration, when an error of type τ occurs: (a) sample p̃_τ ~ Beta(α_τ, β_τ) via Thompson Sampling, (b) allocate fission budget K_τ = round(K_base · (1-p̃_τ) / Z), where Z = Σ_{τ'∈active} (1-p̃_{τ'}) normalizes so total budget matches the uniform baseline, (c) after fission rollouts, update the posterior: α_τ += successes, β_τ += failures. This captures non-stationarity: early in training all types may be hard (high budgets across types), but as the model improves on some types faster than others, budget automatically shifts to the remaining hard types. Unlike static pilot-based allocation (K_τ ∝ 1-RR_pilot(τ)), BAETA's online updates eliminate the need for a separate pilot phase and track the shifting recovery frontier throughout training. We enforce a minimum allocation K_τ ≥ 2 to prevent complete budget starvation for any type. This extends VIP's Bayesian allocation principle from prompt-level (continuous features modeled by Gaussian processes) to error-type level (categorical types modeled by Beta-Bernoulli conjugate pairs), which is a natural and computationally lightweight adaptation—each update is O(1) per error type.\n\nPilot Validation Gate: Before committing to the full experiment, we run 200 trajectories with Qwen3-8B on each benchmark to verify error-type diversity. Requirement: ≥3 error types with n ≥ 30 instances each. If not met on BFCL v4, we augment with deliberate error injection (forcing the model to use incorrect function names or argument types via constrained decoding during a subset of rollouts). If not met on τ-bench, we expand to include the airline domain. We report the pilot distributions transparently.\n\n(2) Error-Type-Stratified Advantage Normalization: Following Stratified GRPO's insight, we stratify GRPO advantages by error type within fission groups: A_stratified(τ_i) = (R(τ_i) - μ_k) / (σ_k + ε), where k is the error type of the fission event. To handle uncertainty in rare types, we use an uncertainty-aware blending coefficient: α_k = min(1, n_k / n_smooth), where n_k is the count for type k and n_smooth = 50 (a hyperparameter). The blended advantage is A_blended = α_k · A_stratified + (1-α_k) · A_global. This naturally reduces to global normalization for rare types (where stratification would be noisy) and full stratification for well-represented types. This extends SAN from structure-based strata (search call count) to error-type strata with principled uncertainty handling.\n\n(3) Controlled Error Feedback: To isolate the effect of type conditioning from error feedback quality, ALL conditions use the same error feedback mechanism—native environment error traces from the benchmark (BFCL v4's structured execution errors; τ-bench's tool execution results). This means our Uniform-Fission baseline is a controlled reimplementation of Fission-GRPO's core mechanism (error-triggered resampling with G' recovery attempts) WITHOUT the Error Simulator, not a reproduction of full Fission-GRPO. We explicitly position this as isolating the type-conditioning question: 'holding error feedback constant, does type-aware allocation and stratification improve recovery?' The Error Simulator (+2.75% on Qwen3-8B per Fission-GRPO's ablation) is an orthogonal contribution that can be combined with BAETA in future work—the two mechanisms are independent.\n\nSystematic Comparison on BFCL v4 Multi-Turn: (a) BAETA (full: Bayesian adaptive budget + type-stratified advantages), (b) Uniform-Fission (uniform G' + global advantages, controlled Fission-GRPO core), (c) Static-ETC (static proportional K_τ from pilot + global advantages, showing Bayesian > static), (d) Stratified-Only (uniform budget + type-stratified advantages, isolating SAN contribution), (e) Standard GRPO (no fission). On τ-bench retail: conditions (a), (b), (e). All conditions use Qwen3-8B with LoRA, 1 iterative training round.\n\nFission-GRPO Reimplementation: Since Fission-GRPO's code is not publicly available (GitHub repository is a placeholder as of May 2026), we reimplement the core fission mechanism from the paper: error detection via execution trace parsing, LIFO buffer for failed trajectories, fission group generation with G'=G=8 recovery attempts per error event, correctness threshold for trajectory acceptance. We use native error traces instead of the Error Simulator for all conditions (see above). We clearly note this is our reimplementation and benchmark against Fission-GRPO's reported numbers where comparable.\n\nExpected Contribution and Null-Result Contingency: We expect BAETA to yield 2-4% absolute improvement over uniform fission on aggregate recovery metrics, driven primarily by improved recovery on hard error types that receive more exploration budget. However, we explicitly frame the paper to be valuable regardless of aggregate improvement magnitude. If BAETA shows no statistically significant aggregate improvement, this itself is an informative result: it would reveal that (a) GRPO's implicit exploration already handles error-type heterogeneity, or (b) error types have more similar recovery difficulty than ToolScan's distributional heterogeneity suggests. The per-type training dynamics analysis—tracking how Beta posteriors, allocated budgets, recovery rates, and advantage signals co-evolve per error type across training—is a novel diagnostic contribution regardless of aggregate outcome. We present this possibility explicitly in the introduction: 'whether the answer is positive or negative, the per-type dynamics analysis informs future RL-based recovery work by revealing the interaction between error heterogeneity and training dynamics.'\n\nPrimary Empirical Contributions: (1) First Bayesian adaptive allocation at error-type level for GRPO-based recovery training, with online updates capturing non-stationarity. (2) First per-error-type training dynamics analysis of RL-based recovery, on two benchmarks with different error taxonomies (BFCL v4: execution-level errors; τ-bench: action-level errors). (3) Controlled comparison isolating type conditioning from error feedback quality.\n\nEvaluation Metrics: Overall accuracy, Recovery Rate (RR), Post-Error Task Success Rate (PE-TSR), Recovery Efficiency (steps-to-recover) following ERR measure.
